title: Australia exposed to economic shocks: S&P
full_text:
The Albanese government's ongoing budget deficits due to record government spending on debt interest, disability and defence have left the nation's finances vulnerable to a negative shock such as a downturn in mining commodity revenues, credit rating agency S&P Global has warned.
S&P sovereign rating analyst Martin Foo said the highest federal spending in 40 years outside the pandemic was working against the Reserve Bank's interest rate rises to tame inflation.
Aggressive spending by states was also pushing up interest payments on their debt to a record $40 billion and adding to inflation pressures as global bond yields soared, said S&P analysts in a briefing following a new report on Australian governments.
The slump in the housing market from the RBA's four interest rate rises and Labor's investor tax changes will also cut state stamp duty revenue by an estimated $8 billion to $10 billion - about 20 per cent - this financial year alone.
While the nation's AAA credit rating was not currently under threat, said Foo, there were two "potential problems" with structural budget deficits and federal spending at its highest outside the pandemic since the 1980s.
"When you think about higher interest payments, higher social security and welfare commitments, higher defence spending, these all look like they're here to stay, and that could be a problem if revenue windfalls decline," he said.
"Some of these windfalls that the government has come to rely on, if they don't materialise, could be an issue," said Foo. "For example, similar to a commodity price shock that we observed in the second half of the last decade."
Foo also said S&P agreed with other economists that high federal and state government spending was "complicating" the job of the RBA. "So right now we have a situation where the RBA and the government are, in some cases, pulling in opposite directions."
The federal budget has reaped a cumulative windfall of more than $400 billion compared to forecasts by Treasury in 2022, due to soaring mining and gas export tax revenue, higher income tax revenue from low unemployment and inflation-induced income tax bracket creep.
Former RBA governor Philip Lowe and former Treasury secretaries Ken Henry and Martin Parkinson have said the budget should be in surplus due to strong tax revenues and to help the RBA fight inflation.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers initially delivered two budget surpluses, followed by two deficits, and last month Treasury's Intergenerational Report projected 40 years of deficits.
Economist Chris Richardson said that federal and state government structural budget deficits left Australia exposed.
"Budget-wise, we will look back on these as good times, but good times that we wasted," he said.
Aaron Wong, an economist with think tank e61, said Treasury's Intergenerational Report had missed the impact of future crises - like the 2008 global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic - that could "knock the budget off course".
"Will the budget have enough room to absorb one or more such shocks in the future?" asked Wong.
Following the 2008 GFC and the end of the first mining revenue boom about four years later, federal government revenue collapsed by about 3 per cent of gross domestic product - the equivalent of $80 billion a year in today's dollars, a drag that persisted through most of the 2010s.
At the state level, the deterioration of public finances in Victoria, Queensland, Tasmania and the ACT were now the biggest concerns, said S&P.
Victoria's $200 billion Suburban Rail Loop and unfunded election commitments in the lead-up to the state's November 28 election could put further pressure on its finances, said S&P's Rebecca Hrvatin.
Combined state government debt is forecast to reach $800 billion this financial year, up from $300 billion before the big spend-up during and after the 2020 pandemic.
